claim: PTBP2 is induced as nestin-positive neuronal progenitors exit mitosis and begin to differentiate.
source: PTBP2 is induced as nestin-positive neuronal progenitors exit mitosis and begin to differentiate (Boutz et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutz et al., 2007

claim: In the embryonic cortex and olfactory bulb, proliferating cells in the subventricular zone are stained for nestin, but more mature cells populating the outer cortical layers have lost nestin expression but gained PTBP2 immunoreactivity.
source: This can be seen in the embryonic cortex and olfactory bulb where proliferating cells in the subventricular zone are stained for nestin, but more mature cells populating the outer cortical layers have lost nestin expression but gained PTBP2 immunoreactivity (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Homozygous Ptbp2 null pups fail to initiate breathing and die due to apparent respiratory failure at birth.
source: Homozygous Ptbp2 null pups generated in subsequent crosses failed to initiate breathing and died due to apparent respiratory failure at birth (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by observational data and image in Figure 1E

claim: Homozygous Ptbp2 null pups do not respond to touch and appear completely paralyzed.
source: Unlike their wild-type or heterozygous littermates, they do not respond to touch and appear completely paralyzed.
evidence: Supported by observational data from the mutant mice

claim: Immunoblots of E18.5 whole brain lysates confirm the complete absence of PTBP2 in homozygous mutant mice and reduced protein in heterozygous mice compared to wild type.
source: Immunoblots of E18.5 whole brain lysates confirm the complete absence of PTBP2 in homozygous mutant mice and reduced protein in heterozygous mice compared to wild type (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The phenotype of the Ptbp2 null allele is consistent with that of another full Ptbp2 null allele.
source: This phenotype is consistent with that of another full Ptbp2 null allele (Licatalosi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Licatalosi et al., 2012

claim: Ptbp2 is expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscle.
source: Since Ptbp2 is also expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscle, defects in these tissues may contribute to the paralysis and death of the germline mutant mice.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: Defects in cardiac and skeletal muscle may contribute to the paralysis and death of the germline mutant mice.
source: Since Ptbp2 is also expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscle, defects in these tissues may contribute to the paralysis and death of the germline mutant mice.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on Ptbp2 expression pattern

claim: Ptbp2-NesKO pups initiated breathing, although at a lower rate than wild type and appeared cyanotic, dying within 1 hr after birth.
source: Unlike the full null, these pups initiated breathing, although at a lower rate than wild type and appeared cyanotic, dying within 1 hr after birth.
evidence: Supported by observational data from Ptbp2-NesKO mice

claim: Immunoblots of E18.5 whole brain from Ptbp2-NesKO pups confirmed the absence of PTBP2 protein.
source: Immunoblots of E18.5 whole brain from Ptbp2-NesKO pups confirmed the absence of PTBP2 protein (Figure 1F, left two lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Both Ptbp2 null and Ptbp2-NesKO embryos were recovered at Mendelian ratios at the late embryonic stage E18.5.
source: Both Ptbp2 null and Ptbp2-NesKO embryos were recovered at Mendelian ratios (27 out of 91, and 12 out of 50) at the late embryonic stage E18.5, suggesting that the lethality was specific to neonates.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from breeding experiments

claim: The lethality of Ptbp2 null and Ptbp2-NesKO mice is specific to neonates.
source: Both Ptbp2 null and Ptbp2-NesKO embryos were recovered at Mendelian ratios (27 out of 91, and 12 out of 50) at the late embryonic stage E18.5, suggesting that the lethality was specific to neonates.
evidence: Inferred from Mendelian ratios at E18.5 and neonatal death

claim: The vast majority of neurons in the CNS of E18.5 Ptbp2LoxP/LoxP/Nestin-Cre brain had lost PTBP2 expression.
source: Immunohistochemistry with PTBP2 antibody on sections of E18.5 Ptbp2LoxP/LoxP/Nestin-Cre brain showed that the vast majority of the neurons in the CNS had lost PTBP2 expression (Figure 2A), while PTBP2 expression in heart and skeletal muscle was unaffected (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A

claim: PTBP2 expression in heart and skeletal muscle was unaffected in Ptbp2LoxP/LoxP/Nestin-Cre mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry with PTBP2 antibody on sections of E18.5 Ptbp2LoxP/LoxP/Nestin-Cre brain showed that the vast majority of the neurons in the CNS had lost PTBP2 expression (Figure 2A), while PTBP2 expression in heart and skeletal muscle was unaffected (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data not shown in the manuscript

claim: Expression of Ptbp1 was not changed in the absence of PTBP2.
source: Expression of Ptbp1, a close paralog of Ptbp2 expressed in neural progenitor cells as well as astrocytes, ependymal cells, and other non-neuronal cell types in the brain, was not changed in the absence of PTBP2 (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data not shown in the manuscript

claim: PTBP2 is not required to maintain PTBP1 repression in post-mitotic neurons where PTBP2 predominates.
source: This suggests that, although PTBP1 can repress PTBP2 expression in cells where PTBP1 is predominant, PTBP2 is not required to maintain PTBP1 repression in post-mitotic neurons where PTBP2 predominates.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ptbp1 expression is unchanged in PTBP2 knockout

claim: Neonatal survival requires PTBP2 expression specifically in the CNS.
source: These results demonstrate that neonatal survival requires PTBP2 expression specifically in the CNS.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotype of Nestin-Cre knockout mice

claim: Ptbp2 mutant embryos showed largely normal morphology for major brain structures such as the neocortex, striatum, hippocampus, and thalamus at E18.5.
source: When stained by Nissl or hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), mutant embryos showed largely normal morphology for major brain structures such as the neocortex, striatum, hippocampus, and thalamus (Figure 2BC).
evidence: Supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: The neocortex of Ptbp2 mutant embryos showed normal thickness and laminar organization at E18.5.
source: The neocortex showed normal thickness and laminar organization (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Immunostaining for a variety of neuronal markers showed no significant differences between mutant and control littermate brains at E18.5.
source: Immunostaining for a variety of neuronal markers, including pan-neuronal markers (Map2, TuJ1), interneuron subtype markers (calbindin and calrectinin), a marker for proliferating nuclei (phosphoHistone3), and for glial and radial glial markers (GFAP and RC2) all showed no significant differences between mutant and control littermate brains (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data not shown in the manuscript

claim: Cortical layer markers (Tbr2, Brn2 and Cux1) showed no significant differences between mutant and control brains at E18.5.
source: To assess possible defects in neuronal migration, we examined cortical layer markers (Tbr2, Brn2 and Cux1) and again did not observe any significant differences between mutant and control brains (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by marker analysis data not shown in the manuscript

claim: Ectopic subventricular mitotic cells were not observed in either the full null or the Ptbp2-NesKO brains.
source: Notably, we did not observe ectopic subventricular mitotic cells in either the full null or the Ptbp2-NesKO brains.
evidence: Supported by observational data from the mutant mice

claim: Ectopic subventricular mitotic cells were previously reported as sporadically occurring in another full germline Ptbp2 null mouse.
source: Such cells were previously reported as sporadically occurring in another full germline Ptbp2 null mouse (Licatalosi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Licatalosi et al., 2012

claim: Different observations regarding ectopic mitotic cells may result from different sensitivity in staining methods or differences in genetic background.
source: These different observations may result from different sensitivity in staining methods or differences in genetic background.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about methodological differences

claim: Several major axonal tracts were either absent or significantly diminished in the Ptbp2 mutant brain at E18.5.
source: Several major axonal tracts were either absent or significantly diminished in the Ptbp2 mutant brain; the internal capsule, external capsule, and the lateral olfactory tract were reduced, and the anterior commissure was absent in the Ptbp2 mutant.
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The internal capsule, external capsule, and the lateral olfactory tract were reduced in the Ptbp2 mutant brain at E18.5.
source: Several major axonal tracts were either absent or significantly diminished in the Ptbp2 mutant brain; the internal capsule, external capsule, and the lateral olfactory tract were reduced, and the anterior commissure was absent in the Ptbp2 mutant.
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The anterior commissure was absent in the Ptbp2 mutant brain at E18.5.
source: Several major axonal tracts were either absent or significantly diminished in the Ptbp2 mutant brain; the internal capsule, external capsule, and the lateral olfactory tract were reduced, and the anterior commissure was absent in the Ptbp2 mutant.
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Major axonal tracts connect distant regions of the developing brain, such as cortex, thalamus, and the brainstem, and are essential to basic physiological functions such as respiratory control.
source: These major axonal tracts connect distant regions of the developing brain, such as cortex, thalamus, and the brainstem, and are essential to basic physiological functions such as respiratory control.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuroanatomy

claim: Axonal defects may contribute to the neonatal lethal phenotype of Ptbp2 mutant mice.
source: These axonal defects may thus contribute to the neonatal lethal phenotype.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed axonal defects

claim: PTBP2 expression goes down during the first postnatal week of brain development with moderate levels maintained into adulthood.
source: PTBP2 expression goes down during the first postnatal week of brain development with moderate levels maintained into adulthood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies

claim: PSD95 (Dlg4) shows changes in splicing coincident with the postnatal depletion of PTBP2.
source: Identified PTBP2 targets such as PSD95 (Dlg4) show changes in splicing coincident with this postnatal depletion of PTBP2 (Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2012

claim: In Ptbp2loxP/loxP:Emx1-Cre+/− mice, Ptbp2 is highly depleted from the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and olfactory bulb, but still expressed at high levels in other brain regions.
source: In Ptbp2loxP/loxP:Emx1-Cre+/− mice (Ptbp2-EmxKO), Ptbp2 is highly depleted from the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and olfactory bulb, but still expressed at high levels in other brain regions, such as cerebellum, striatum, and brain stem (Figure 3AB and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Ptbp2-EmxKO pups were viable, with body weights similar to control newborns at P0.
source: Unlike the Nestin and Germline-Cre knockouts, Ptbp2-EmxKO pups were viable, with body weights similar to control newborns at P0.
evidence: Supported by observational data from Ptbp2-EmxKO mice

claim: Ptbp2-EmxKO mutant mice displayed slower growth than their littermates and could be identified by their small size and low body weight as early as postnatal day 3.
source: However, these mutant mice displayed slower growth than their littermates and could be identified by their small size and low body weight as early as postnatal day 3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by observational data and image shown in Figure 3A

claim: By P14, the average weight of Ptbp2-EmxKO mice was less than half of control pups.
source: By P14, their average weight was less than half of control pups, and they all died around weaning age (P18-21).
evidence: Supported by quantitative weight measurements

claim: Ptbp2-EmxKO mice all died around weaning age (P18-21).
source: By P14, their average weight was less than half of control pups, and they all died around weaning age (P18-21).
evidence: Supported by observational data from Ptbp2-EmxKO mice

claim: The Ptbp2-EmxKO cortex appeared relatively normal at birth.
source: The Ptbp2-EmxKO cortex appeared relatively normal at birth.
evidence: Supported by observational data from Ptbp2-EmxKO mice

claim: While control cortices thicken and grow in size during the first three postnatal weeks, the EmxKO cortex displayed widespread neuronal death and degeneration.
source: However, while the control cortices thicken and grow in size during the first three postnatal weeks, largely due to development of the neuropil and white matter, the EmxKO cortex displayed widespread neuronal death and degeneration (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3C-E

claim: Brain structures not subject to PTBP2 loss, such as striatum, developed normally in Ptbp2-EmxKO mice.
source: Brain structures not subject to PTBP2 loss, such as striatum, developed normally.
evidence: Supported by observational data from Ptbp2-EmxKO mice

claim: At P5, the EmxKO cortex was substantially thinner than control cortices.
source: Comparing coronal sections of mutant and control brains at P5, the EmxKO cortex was substantially thinner than control cortices.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Nissl staining revealed widespread pyknotic nuclei within the EmxKO cortical plate at P5 as a result of neuronal cell death.
source: Nissl staining revealed widespread pyknotic nuclei within the EmxKO cortical plate as a result of neuronal cell death (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 3D

claim: By P11, the EmxKO cortex had further degenerated with additional loss of tissue integrity.
source: By P11, when control cortex had substantially thickened with well-defined cellular layers, the EmxKO cortex had further degenerated with additional loss of tissue integrity.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The lateral ventricles were enlarged in EmxKO brains at both P5 and P11.
source: The lateral ventricles were enlarged in EmxKO brains at both P5 and P11, and the corpus callosum was missing (Figure 3E and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The corpus callosum was missing in EmxKO brains.
source: The lateral ventricles were enlarged in EmxKO brains at both P5 and P11, and the corpus callosum was missing (Figure 3E and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The mutant hippocampus was significantly reduced in size in Ptbp2-EmxKO mice.
source: Other brain structures where Ptbp2 was inactivated were also defective in the EmxKO; the mutant hippocampus was significantly reduced in size and the lamination in the olfactory bulb was highly disrupted, with the Mitral cell layer entirely absent (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data not shown in the manuscript

claim: The lamination in the olfactory bulb was highly disrupted in Ptbp2-EmxKO mice, with the Mitral cell layer entirely absent.
source: Other brain structures where Ptbp2 was inactivated were also defective in the EmxKO; the mutant hippocampus was significantly reduced in size and the lamination in the olfactory bulb was highly disrupted, with the Mitral cell layer entirely absent (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data not shown in the manuscript

claim: The postnatal lethality of Ptbp2-EmxKO mice demonstrates a continued requirement for PTBP2 to allow neuronal maturation and survival in the developing postnatal cortex.
source: The postnatal lethality of Ptbp2-EmxKO mice demonstrates a continued requirement for PTBP2 to allow neuronal maturation and survival in the developing postnatal cortex.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotype of Ptbp2-EmxKO mice

claim: The survival of Ptbp2-EmxKO mice past birth suggests that the neonatal lethality of Ptbp2 null and NesKO mice is due to loss of PTBP2 in early maturing regions of the CNS critical for basic physiological function in the neonate.
source: The survival of these mice past birth suggests that the neonatal lethality of Ptbp2 null and NesKO mice is due to loss of PTBP2 in early maturing regions of the CNS critical for basic physiological function in the neonate.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of different knockout phenotypes

claim: The mutant brains of E18 Ptbp2 null mice exhibited strikingly lower levels of multiple synaptic markers.
source: The mutant brains exhibited strikingly lower levels of multiple synaptic markers (Figure 4A), including PSD95, the neurotransmitter receptor NR2B, the major synaptic vesicle protein Synaptophysin (SYP), and the trans-synaptic scaffolding protein Neuroligin1 (NLG1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Synaptic markers including PSD95, NR2B, Synaptophysin (SYP), and Neuroligin1 (NLG1) were reduced in E18 Ptbp2 null brains.
source: The mutant brains exhibited strikingly lower levels of multiple synaptic markers (Figure 4A), including PSD95, the neurotransmitter receptor NR2B, the major synaptic vesicle protein Synaptophysin (SYP), and the trans-synaptic scaffolding protein Neuroligin1 (NLG1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Other synaptic proteins, such as Cask and GluR2, also declined in E18 Ptbp2 null brains.
source: Other synaptic proteins, such as the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase Cask and the Glutamate Receptor GluR2 also declined.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Cells may be arrested or delayed in their maturation or synapse formation may be otherwise defective in the absence of PTBP2.
source: These results indicate that cells may be arrested or delayed in their maturation or that synapse formation may be otherwise defective in the absence of PTBP2.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in synaptic protein levels

claim: Heterozygous Ptbp2+/− mouse brains express the PTBP2 protein at about half normal levels.
source: Interestingly, heterozygous Ptbp2+/− mouse brains express the PTBP2 protein at about half normal levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The effect of partial PTBP2 depletion on synaptic protein expression and on splicing of target transcripts was variable in heterozygous mice.
source: The effect of this partial depletion on synaptic protein expression and on splicing of target transcripts was variable (Figure 4A, and see below).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and splicing data

claim: For some targets, protein levels in the heterozygous brains were intermediate between the wild type and homozygous knockout.
source: For some targets, protein levels in the heterozygous brains were intermediate between the wild type and homozygous knockout (GluR2 and NR2B, Figure 4A, also see CamKinase 2b below).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In some cases, the heterozygote appeared similar to the wild-type mice, expressing close to normal levels of PSD95, Synaptophysin, Neuroligin1, and Cask.
source: In other cases, the heterozygote appeared similar to the wild-type mice, expressing close to normal levels of PSD95, Synaptophysin, Neuroligin1, and Cask.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: A single copy of Ptbp2 is sufficient to support development.
source: Given that Ptbp2 heterozygous mice are viable, a single copy of Ptbp2 is apparently sufficient to support development.
evidence: Inferred from the viability of heterozygous mice

claim: Dissociated mouse neurons cultured in vitro progress through several stages of maturation that parallel their in vivo development.
source: Dissociated mouse neurons cultured in vitro progress through several stages of maturation that parallel their in vivo development (Dotti et al., 1988; Palmer et al., 1997; Arimura and Kaibuchi, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dotti et al., 1988; Palmer et al., 1997; Arimura and Kaibuchi, 2007

claim: Immediately after dissociation and plating, cortical neurons from E15-16 Ptbp2-NesKO mice exhibited similar viability to control neurons.
source: Immediately after dissociation and plating, cortical neurons from E15-16 Ptbp2-NesKO mice exhibited similar viability to control neurons.
evidence: Supported by observational data from cultured neurons

claim: Ptbp2-KO neurons grew extensive neurites during the first week in culture and were indistinguishable from control cultures when stained with the dendritic marker MAP2.
source: The Ptbp2-KO neurons grew extensive neurites during the first week in culture and were indistinguishable from control cultures when stained with the dendritic marker MAP2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B

claim: During the second week, increased signs of neuronal death appear in cultures of Ptbp2-KO neurons.
source: However during the second week, increased signs of neuronal death appear in cultures of Ptbp2-KO neurons, including neurite retraction, membrane blebbing and shrinkage, and nuclear condensation.
evidence: Supported by observational data from cultured neurons

claim: All neurons lacking PTBP2 die by the end of third week of culture.
source: All neurons lacking PTBP2 die by the end of third week of culture.
evidence: Supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: A similar catastrophic cell death occurred during the third week of culture in hippocampal neurons cultured from E18 Ptbp2 null mice.
source: A similar catastrophic cell death occurred during the third week of culture in hippocampal neurons cultured from E18 Ptbp2 null mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The timing and scale of the neuronal death in culture is similar to the wide-spread degeneration seen in the postnatal (P5-P11) Emx-KO brains.
source: The timing and scale of the neuronal death in culture is similar to the wide-spread degeneration seen in the postnatal (P5-P11) Emx-KO brains.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of in vitro and in vivo phenotypes

claim: Both in vivo and in vitro, PTBP2 is clearly required for the survival of forebrain neurons.
source: Both in vivo and in vitro, PTBP2 is clearly required for the survival of forebrain neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the cell death phenotypes observed in vivo and in vitro

claim: Splicing regulators generally have many target transcripts.
source: Splicing regulators generally have many target transcripts and it is expected that the dramatic phenotype of PTBP2 loss will be derived from multiple deficits.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of splicing regulators

claim: The dramatic phenotype of PTBP2 loss is expected to be derived from multiple deficits.
source: Splicing regulators generally have many target transcripts and it is expected that the dramatic phenotype of PTBP2 loss will be derived from multiple deficits.
evidence: Inferred from the general properties of splicing regulators

claim: Transcriptome-wide analyses identified a large set of cassette exons and other alternative splicing events that are mis-regulated in developing (E18) Ptbp2−/− brains.
source: These analyses identified a large set of cassette exons and other alternative splicing events that are mis-regulated in developing (E18) Ptbp2−/− brains (Supplementary files 1–3 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by microarray and RNAseq data

claim: 359 PTBP2 target cassette exons were identified by microarray analysis.
source: Using cutoffs of a Sepscore of 0.345 for the arrays and a 10% change in PSI for the RNAseq, we identified 359 PTBP2 target cassette exons by array (Supplementary file 2 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014])) and 597 exons by RNAseq (Supplementary file 3 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis

claim: 597 PTBP2 target cassette exons were identified by RNAseq.
source: Using cutoffs of a Sepscore of 0.345 for the arrays and a 10% change in PSI for the RNAseq, we identified 359 PTBP2 target cassette exons by array (Supplementary file 2 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014])) and 597 exons by RNAseq (Supplementary file 3 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: 92 exons were found by both microarray and RNAseq methods.
source: These included 92 exons found by both methods.
evidence: Supported by comparison of microarray and RNAseq data

claim: A large set of splicing events was validated by RT-PCR (77 out of 88).
source: Assaying additional control and mutant mice as biological replicates, a large set of splicing events was further validated by RT-PCR (77 out of 88; Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Both the array and RNAseq methods yielded validation rates above 70%.
source: Both the array and RNAseq methods yielded validation rates above 70%.
evidence: Calculated from RT-PCR validation data

claim: The majority of identified cassette exons (379 of 597 from the RNAseq analysis) showed increased splicing in the absence of PTBP2.
source: The majority of identified cassette exons (379 of 597 from the RNAseq analysis) showed increased splicing in the absence of PTBP2 (Supplementary file 3 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]), suggesting that PTBP2 functions more often as a splicing repressor than as a splicing activator, similar to the observations of PTBP1 (Keppetipola et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis

claim: PTBP2 functions more often as a splicing repressor than as a splicing activator, similar to the observations of PTBP1.
source: The majority of identified cassette exons (379 of 597 from the RNAseq analysis) showed increased splicing in the absence of PTBP2 (Supplementary file 3 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]), suggesting that PTBP2 functions more often as a splicing repressor than as a splicing activator, similar to the observations of PTBP1 (Keppetipola et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the predominance of increased splicing in the knockout and supported by citation to Keppetipola et al., 2012

claim: Altered splicing was observed in many known direct PTBP1/PTBP2 targets including PSD95 (Dlg4), Atp2b1, Bin1, Dst and Fn1.
source: Altered splicing was observed in many known direct PTBP1/PTBP2 targets including PSD95 (Dlg4), Atp2b1, Bin1, Dst and Fn1 (Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012

claim: For exons whose percent-spliced-in value (PSI) changed by more than 20% in the knockout, approximately 70% have significant PTBP2 CLIP clusters in their adjacent introns in E18 mouse brain.
source: For exons whose percent-spliced-in value (PSI) changed by more than 20% in the knockout, approximately 70% are reported to have significant PTBP2 CLIP clusters in their adjacent introns in E18 mouse brain (Licatalosi et al., 2012) (SZ unpublished data).
evidence: Supported by citation to Licatalosi et al., 2012 and unpublished data

claim: Exons in Agrn, Arhgef7, Dbn1, Erc1 and Sorbs2, whose splicing is altered in the PTBP2−/− brain and which are also expressed in HeLa cells, were also identified as PTBP1 targets in a HeLa CLIP analysis.
source: Exons in Agrn, Arhgef7, Dbn1, Erc1 and Sorbs2, whose splicing is altered in the PTBP2−/− brain and which are also expressed in HeLa cells, were also identified as PTBP1 targets in a HeLa CLIP analysis (Xue et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xue et al., 2009

claim: The majority of isoform changes identified in the knockout are likely to be directly regulated by PTBP2.
source: These data indicate that the majority of isoform changes identified in the knockout are likely to be directly regulated by PTBP2.

claim: Some splicing changes in the analyzed brains will be indirect effects of other changes in the developing mice.
source: Nevertheless, it should be noted that the analyzed brains developed to E18 in the absence of PTBP2 and it is expected that some splicing changes will be indirect effects of other changes in the developing mice.

claim: Validated PTBP2-dependent splicing events include many transcripts with important neuronal functions.
source: Validated PTBP2-dependent splicing events include many transcripts with important neuronal functions, including the postsynaptic scaffolding proteins PSD95 (Dlg4) and gephryn (Gphn), the neurotransmitter receptor GABAA Rγ2 (Gabg2), and the key calcium signaling molecules CamK2a and CamK2b (Figure 5AB, Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Li et al., 2014).

claim: Biological Process annotations that were significantly enriched in the PTBP2 target set (p<0.001) included 'regulation of transcription', 'synaptic transmission', 'transmission of nerve impulse', 'synapse organization', 'cell morphogenesis', 'endocytosis', and 'neuron projection development'.
source: Biological Process annotations that were significantly enriched in the PTBP2 target set (p<0.001) included 'regulation of transcription', 'synaptic transmission', 'transmission of nerve impulse', 'synapse organization', 'cell morphogenesis', 'endocytosis', and 'neuron projection development' (Supplementary file 4 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNAseq data

claim: All of the enriched biological process functions are dynamically changing during the period of neuronal maturation when PTBP2-dependent defects are observed.
source: All of these functions are dynamically changing during the period of neuronal maturation when PTBP2-dependent defects are observed.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuronal development

claim: Some transcripts are likely to be reduced through direct PTBP2 effects on post-transcriptional processes.
source: Some of these transcripts are likely to be reduced through direct PTBP2 effects on post-transcriptional processes.
evidence: Inferred from the nature of PTBP2 function

claim: Five transcripts containing PTBP2-dependent exons with mapped CLIP clusters have changes in splicing predicted to lead to nonsense mediated decay.
source: These include five transcripts containing PTBP2-dependent exons with mapped CLIP clusters whose change in splicing is predicted to lead to nonsense mediated decay.

claim: Other changes in transcript expression are likely to be an indirect result of developmental defects associated with the loss of PTBP2.
source: Other changes in transcript expression are likely to be an indirect result of developmental defects associated with the loss of PTBP2.

source: Relative to all transcripts expressed in wild-type brains, upregulated transcripts were highly enriched for GO terms associated with innate immunity and the inflammatory response (p<0.001).

claim: The functional enrichments for innate immunity and inflammatory response likely result from the degeneration seen in the Ptbp2 knockout brains, rather than direct PTBP2 targeting of the transcripts.
source: Given the phenotype of the mice, these functional enrichments likely result from the degeneration seen in the Ptbp2 knockout brains, rather than direct PTBP2 targeting of the transcripts.

claim: Down-regulated transcripts were only weakly enriched for particular bioprocess terms.
source: Down-regulated transcripts were only weakly enriched for particular bioprocess terms.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNAseq data

claim: Only terms related to cell adhesion had enrichment p values below 0.01 among down-regulated transcripts.
source: Only terms related to cell adhesion had enrichment p values below 0.01.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNAseq data

claim: Many of the identified PTBP2 targets display a common pattern of temporal regulation in the developing wild-type brain.
source: We find that many of the identified PTBP2 targets display a common pattern of temporal regulation in the developing wild-type brain.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR analysis across developmental timepoints

claim: PTBP2 target transcripts contain exons that are mostly excluded in the embryonic brain and whose splicing increases during the first 3 weeks after birth.
source: These transcripts contain exons that are mostly excluded in the embryonic brain and whose splicing increases during the first 3 weeks after birth (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 in Dryad [Li et al., 2014]).

claim: The normal shift in splicing of PTBP2 target transcripts coincides with the known postnatal decrease in PTBP2 levels in the brain.

claim: PTBP2 continues to be present at moderate levels into adulthood after being reduced in expression after differentiation.
source: Although reduced in expression after differentiation, PTBP2 continues to be present at moderate levels into adulthood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies

claim: Remaining PTBP2 in adult neurons may serve to maintain the partial repression of some exons.

evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the continued presence of PTBP2 in adults

claim: In addition to the precocious expression of adult isoforms, the deleterious effect of PTBP2 loss may also result from the aberrantly high expression of isoforms normally present at lower levels.
